newsitem.title: UK: Lloyd's of London outlines infrastructure changes.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd's of London outlines infrastructure changes.

text.p: Lloyds of London on Thursday unveiled plans to reshape the insurance market's core infrastructure operations, but gave no details of potential cost savings or job cuts.

"This creates the platform from which further efficiencies can be obtained...I anticipate that there will be job losses," chief executive Ron Sandler told a news conference, but declined to say how many jobs may go.
The changes are intended to give the Corporation's service operations a distinct commercial focus and improve the market's competitiveness, Lloyd's said in a statement.
At the heart of the reforms is the creation of five business units and the introduction of user boards for each unit, which will be set up with effect from January 1, 1997.
The five units are members' services, insurance services, facilities management, business development and North America. All five will report to the Lloyd's Market Board.
The aim behind the business units is that they should operate on the user pays principle and "align the Corporation more closely with the business objectives of the market," Sandler said.
"The centre is hard to understand...and that has led to a lack of efficiency and accountability," he added.
The units will lead to greater transparency of activities, greater accountability to users, greater responsiveness to market need and greater choice of service providers, Lloyd's said.

Lloyd's central costs are currently in the region of 180 million stg a year and the Corporation has 2,400 employees, including 415 who are contractors or consultants involved in the market's Reconstruction and Renewal (R&R) programme.

The implementation of key parts of R&R in recent months has put the bulk of Lloyd's past problems behind it and allowed the Corporation to concentrate on the current strategy for internal reform, Sandler said.
Some Corporation functions -- finance, strategic planning, human resources, legal services and communications -- will remain under central control.
The future of regulation will be decided by a review announced last month and due to be completed by mid-1997.

Sandler said there would be opportunities for selling some services outside Lloyd's, but noted that consideration had to be given to the legal framework and the needs of the rest of the London Market.

Lloyd's has for some time been discussing joint initiatives with the other main insurance service providers in London -- the Institute of London Underwriters (ILU) and the London International Insurance and Reinsurance Market Association (LIRMA).
